content: The MS Bike Tour, also known as the MS 150, is a series of charity cycling events organized by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. These events take place in various locations across the United States, Canada, and Australia. The primary goal of these rides is to raise funds for multiple sclerosis (MS) research conducted by the National MS Society. In the United States, the rides are branded as MS 150 and typically span two days, covering approximately 150 miles, although shorter one-day rides are also available. The routes are designed to start and end in major cities to maximize accessibility for participants. The number of participants varies significantly by event, with some rides, such as the Houston-to-Austin route, capped at 13,000 riders in 2006 to prevent overcrowding. In Australia, the event is called Sydney to the Gong, referring to the city of Wollongong, located 90 kilometers south of Sydney. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system (CNS). It involves the deterioration of myelin, the protective sheath surrounding nerve fibers in the CNS, leading to the formation of lesions known as sclerosis. MS presents with a wide range of symptoms, including vision loss, paralysis, numbness, and walking difficulties, which can be unpredictable and episodic. These symptoms often complicate the diagnostic process. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society, established in 1946, is dedicated to combating MS by funding research, providing services for individuals with MS, offering professional education programs, and advocating for MS-related issues. The MS Bike Tours are one of the organization's more recent initiatives, having started approximately 22 years ago in select cities. These tours have become one of the largest fundraising events for the MS Society, now occurring in 48 states and several locations in Canada. The length of the tours varies, ranging from 30 miles to 180 miles. Participants can contribute by cycling, volunteering, or pledging financial support. The events aim to foster community involvement by engaging local businesses, elected officials, residents, and individuals living with MS. Typically, 75% of the funds raised go directly toward research. In North America, around 48 state chapters support the MS Bike Tours annually. In 2006, over 100,000 participants raised $67 million for the organization. The tours continue to grow in popularity, with over 100 events held between April and November each year. Each tour is unique, with individual chapters determining the length, date, and location of their events. The largest bike tour is hosted by the Lone Star Chapter in Texas. To date, the Lone Star Chapter's MS 150 Bike Tours have raised over $47 million for the National MS Society. This chapter organizes three two-day events annually, starting with the BP MS 150 in April, which runs from Houston to Austin. This ride is the largest of its kind in North America and the largest non-profit sporting event in Texas. The Sam’s Club MS 150 follows in May, running from Frisco to Fort Worth, and the Valero MS 150 takes place in October, running from San Antonio to Corpus Christi. These events strategically target major cities to attract media attention and public support. In Australia, the annual event offers two distance options: a 90-kilometer ride from St. Peters in Sydney Park to Stuart Park in Wollongong, and a shorter 56-kilometer ride from Heathcote High School to Stuart Park. In 2007, the event was held on November 4th. In 2006, 100,000 riders participated in the MS Bike Tours, collectively raising $67 million to support the fight against MS. Riders face the physical and emotional challenge of enduring the ride while contributing to the cause. Participants range in age from as young as six to as old as 82. Most riders use traditional street-racing bicycles, but some prefer tandem or recumbent bikes, hand-operated cycles, or even unicycles. Any bike is acceptable as long as it does not pose a safety risk to the rider or others. Depending on the terrain, certain types of bicycles may perform better than others. Rider safety is a top priority, and all tours must adhere to the National MS Society's safety guidelines as well as state and local laws. Roads and trails are secured for the riders before the event, and breaking certain rules can result in immediate removal from the event. Helmets are mandatory to prevent head injuries in case of accidents. Police and volunteers are stationed along the route with HAM radios and safety kits to assist riders in need. Rest stops are equipped with minor medical services, refreshments, technical support, and bathrooms. Riders are required to pledge a minimum fundraising amount to participate, which varies by chapter, ranging from $125 to $350. To encourage higher fundraising efforts, some chapters have special clubs for top fundraisers. The National MS Society has also introduced a program called Champions Against MS, which pairs riders with local individuals living with MS. Riders receive signed bandanas from their buddies to display their support. Volunteers play a crucial role in the success of these events, often matching the number of riders. They help with event setup, cleanup, and various tasks throughout the event, such as cooking, providing massages, or assisting with bike racks. Volunteers also ensure rider safety and comfort by offering support and gear (SAG) services, minor medical attention, traffic control, and route patrol. HAM radio operators are often recruited to establish a communications network along the route. Volunteers are known for their energetic and supportive demeanor, often dressing in colorful outfits and using noise-makers to encourage riders. Their enthusiasm provides a morale boost for participants at every stop and along the route. Celebrity involvement has also been a significant aspect of the MS Bike Tours. Country singer Clay Walker, diagnosed with MS in 1996, participates in the annual BP MS 150 and inspires others with MS to pursue their goals. Texas Governor Rick Perry and Houston Mayor Bill White participated in the Texas BP MS 150 in 2004, with White completing the entire ride and Perry joining for the final 10 miles. National talk show host Montel Williams, who revealed his MS diagnosis in 1999, has founded his own MS bike tour in New York, a 20-mile ride open to the public in Sag Harbor. Many tours also feature local celebrities, including government officials, media personalities, and prominent business figures. Corporate sponsors provide substantial support for the MS Bike Tours, contributing significantly to the funds raised. Sponsors range from large corporations to local businesses, helping to unite communities in the fight against MS. Sponsorship levels include title sponsors, platinum, gold, silver, and bronze sponsors. Other sponsors, such as radio stations, transportation companies, and hotels, often provide services in addition to financial contributions. For example, radio and television stations send personalities to play music and announce riders at the finish line, transportation companies offer shuttles, and hotels provide discounted accommodations. Riders representing sponsor companies often wear jerseys displaying the sponsor's name. Many sponsors also set up tents at the finish lines, offering food, beverages, and amenities like massages for their riders.
